title: Kth Smallest Element
directAnswer: Sort ascending and return `nums[k-1]`. O(n log n). For large data, quickselect is O(n) average and a min-heap is O(n + k log n).

remember.takeaway: k-th smallest = sort and index; quickselect if you need speed.
antiSignals: Streaming / huge data — use a bounded heap or quickselect

problemStatement: Given an integer array `nums` and `k` (1-indexed), return the k-th smallest element.
understanding: Sorting and indexing at k-1 is the simple O(n log n) answer; a heap or quickselect can do better.

approaches.name: Sort and index
approaches.whenToMention: This is the standard, expected solution — lead with it.
approaches.explanation:
The k-th smallest element sits at index k−1 once the array is sorted, so **sort and index** is the clean O(n log n) baseline. Faster methods exist for a single order statistic.

**Why sort-and-index is correct.** Sorting ascending arranges elements by rank; the element at 0-based index k−1 is the k-th smallest (1-indexed k). Duplicates count toward the rank, which is the usual convention.

**Why mention quickselect / a heap.** If you only need one order statistic, sorting everything is overkill. **Quickselect** partitions like quicksort but recurses into only one side, averaging O(n). A bounded **max-heap of size k** gives O(n log k). Naming these shows you know sorting isn't always necessary.

**Don't mutate the caller's array** unless allowed — sort a copy.

code.python:
def kth_smallest(nums: list[int], k: int) -> int:
    return sorted(nums)[k - 1]

approaches.insight: Naming quickselect / a bounded heap shows you know sorting isn't always necessary for a single order statistic.
approaches.complexityReasoning: sorting is O(n log n); quickselect averages O(n); a size-k heap is O(n log k).
